tagline.text: A 7km sandbar that appears at low tide, with stilt cottages perched over the sea

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,000–3,000 per person (per day, sharing a boat)

children.text: A roughly 7km white sandbar that appears only at low tide near the mouth of Bais Bay on eastern Negros Island. Its stilt cottages, which seem to float on the sea, have earned it the nickname "the Maldives of the Philippines." Most visitors pair it with a day-long boat tour that includes dolphin watching in the Tañon Strait.
Manjuyod Sandbar is a long strip of sand lying in the Tañon Strait between Cebu and Negros islands, at the mouth of northern Bais Bay in Negros Oriental. It sits about
north of Dumaguete, and although it administratively belongs to Manjuyod, most travelers reach it by boat from a pier in neighboring Bais City. The sandbar stretches roughly
7km
in length but is narrow, so it is nearly submerged at high tide and re-emerges as a long white strip in the middle of the sea once the tide goes out.

A handful of wooden cottages stand on stilts above the sandbar. At high tide they appear to float on emerald water; at low tide they stand tall on bare sand, evoking the over-water villas of the Maldives. As photos of this scene spread on social media, the sandbar earned the nickname "the Maldives of the Philippines" and has since become one of Negros Oriental's signature photo spots.

The Tañon Strait, where the sandbar lies, is one of the largest marine protected areas in the Philippines, and pods of dolphins, including spinner dolphins, often appear here. Bais boat tours are typically built around this rhythm: spot dolphins in the strait early in the morning, then swim and relax on the sandbar, and stop at a mangrove forest on the way back. Bais grew into a sugar town around a large mill that opened in
, so visitors can still see lodging housed in old mill-company buildings and views of sugarcane fields.

There are almost no facilities, which keeps it peaceful, and the shallow water is easy for children to wade and play in. It makes a good day trip for travelers based in Dumaguete, and suits couples, families, and friends who enjoy photography and the sea. Because the sandbar only appears on the tide's schedule, though, you need to plan carefully to enjoy it properly.

blocks.title: Walking the Sandbar at Low Tide

children.text: When the water pulls back, walk out onto white sand that stretches so far the end disappears from view. The way the water color shifts from jade to deep blue on either side is the highlight.

The cottages perched on stilts over the water are the symbol of Manjuyod. Afloat at high tide and standing on bare sand at low tide, they let you capture completely different photos from the same spot.

blocks.title: Dolphin Watching in the Tañon Strait

children.text: Head out into the strait by boat early in the morning to look for pods of dolphins. With luck you'll see them leaping beside the bow, but since they're wild animals, a sighting is never guaranteed.

blocks.title: Swimming and Snorkeling in Shallow Water

children.text: The water around the sandbar is clear and shallow, making it good for swimming. You can spot starfish and small fish on the seagrass beds and sandy bottom — just watch, and don't take them out of the water.
On the way back, stop at the Talabong Mangrove Forest Reserve in Bais Bay and walk its bamboo boardwalk. You can see waterbirds and the mangrove ecosystem up close.
The local way to eat is to buy seafood and a packed lunch in Bais and eat it in a cottage or on the boat. Ask your boatman in advance whether he can grill it for you.

blocks.title: A Night in a Stilt Cottage

children.text: You can book a stay in a stilt cottage through the tourism office. Electricity and facilities are minimal, but watching the sunset and starry sky from the middle of the sea is a special experience.

This schedule assumes low tide falls in the morning. Check a tide table and adjust the order of dolphin watching and the sandbar visit to match whenever the sandbar is most exposed.
Manila to Sibulan Airport (DGT) in Dumaguete takes about
1 hour 20 minutes
. The airport sits north of Dumaguete in Sibulan, which makes it convenient for heading toward Bais — about
1 hour
by car from the airport to Bais.
From Cebu, another option is to take a ferry (about
20–30 minutes
) from Liloan port at the southern tip of Cebu Island to Sibulan, then head north to Bais.
Buses bound for Bais and San Carlos leave frequently from the Ceres bus terminal in Dumaguete. The trip to Bais takes about
1 hour to 1 hour 30 minutes
, and the fare is about
From downtown Bais, it's about
10–15 minutes
by tricycle to Capiñahan Pier or Canibol Pier.
Charter a whole boat at the pier. A full-day rental combining dolphin watching and the sandbar runs about
for a boat of 5–7 people, and the fare rises if you need a bigger boat for more passengers. A registration fee or environmental fee may be added separately.
It takes about
30–45 minutes
from the pier to the sandbar. Boats can also be chartered from the Manjuyod side of the coast, so ask at your accommodation or the tourism office.
Travel agencies and accommodations in Dumaguete can arrange a package tour with round-trip transport, a boat, and lunch, priced at about
per person depending on group size. It's convenient for families who'd rather not switch between public transport options.
The dry season,
December–May
, is best.
March–May
in particular brings calm seas and clear skies for the most vivid views of the sandbar and water, though the lack of shade can push the midday heat index close to
. The Tañon Strait sits between Cebu and Negros islands, which shields it somewhat from wind, so boat trips here tend to run more reliably year-round than on other stretches of coast.
June–November

is the rainy season, with frequent overcast skies and showers, and boats won't sail if a typhoon signal is raised. More important than the season, though, is the tide on the day of your visit. Choose a day when low tide falls in the morning so the sandbar is widely exposed; dolphins also tend to be easier to spot in the early morning, so a morning low tide is ideal. Around the full moon and new moon, the tidal range is larger and the sandbar is exposed even more widely.

Most travelers stay in Dumaguete, which has plenty of restaurants and lodging, and visit as a day trip. Around Rizal Boulevard in Dumaguete there are many hotels and guesthouses priced around

a night. If you want to catch an early boat, spending a night in Bais is also a good option. Bais has long-running places to stay, such as La Planta Hotel, converted from an old sugar-mill company building, as well as small pensions. Stilt-cottage stays on the sandbar can only be booked through the Bais or Manjuyod tourism office, and the facilities are very basic.

There are no shops on the sandbar, so you must bring your own lunch, water, and snacks. You can buy grilled fish, shrimp, squid, and rice at the Bais market, or prepare a packed lunch in Dumaguete. Back in Dumaguete, try the old cafes in the Silliman University area, the barbecue at Rizal Boulevard stalls, and Dumaguete's signature dessert, silvanas. Crab and fish dishes from the seas around Bais are also cheap at local restaurants, but for shellfish, check the wastewater spill notice under the cautions first.
Be sure to check the Bais-area tide table before you set out. If you miss the low-tide window, the sandbar will barely be visible.
To see dolphins, it's best to leave the pier around
6–7 AM
. Dolphins tend to scatter into deeper water as the sun climbs higher.
Boats are chartered by the boat, not the seat, so gathering companions through your Dumaguete accommodation or a travel community can cut the per-person cost significantly.
Before hiring a boat, clearly agree on whether dolphin watching, time on the sandbar, and the mangrove visit are included, and settle the total duration.
There is no shade at all. Bring a hat, sunglasses, a rash guard, reef-safe sunscreen, and plenty of water.
Keep your phone in a waterproof pouch — drone footage looks most dramatic when the sandbar is widely exposed at low tide.
Buses back to Dumaguete become infrequent in the evening, so plan to leave Bais by mid-afternoon at the latest.
As the tide comes in, the sandbar submerges quickly. Don't walk far out toward the end of the sandbar — stay within sight of the boat and boatman, and follow instructions to return.
Taking starfish out of the water to photograph them can kill them. Observe marine life with your eyes only, underwater.
Don't chase or feed the dolphins, and ask your boatman not to bring the boat too close to a pod.
Sea urchins or sharp shells can hide among the seagrass, so wearing aqua shoes is the safer choice.
Boat fares, registration fees, and cottage-use rules change often at the local government's discretion. Check the latest notices from the Bais or Manjuyod tourism office before you visit.
Take all your trash with you, and don't lean on or climb onto the stilt-cottage railings.
A dike at the retention pond of an ethanol plant in Bais collapsed, and wastewater flowed into North Bais Bay and the Tañon Strait, closing the sandbar from
October 28 to November 19, 2025
. It has reopened, but a Silliman University survey in
July 2026

found that about 70% of the coral in Bais Bay had died, and a ban on shellfish gathering also continued for some time. If the water is murky or smells, avoid swimming, and check the latest notices from the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) and local governments for seafood and shellfish.
